Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Kelepi, a sixty-five-year-old project manager with a quiet authority that had served him well for decades, now found his life governed by a rigid, unspoken set of rules. It had been two years since his son, Manu, had recovered, but for Kelepi, the crisis had never truly ended. The night it happened plays on a continuous loop in his mind, not as a coherent story, but as a series of sensory fragments. The worst part, the part that ambushes him in the quiet of his office, was the sound—a thin, high-pitched wheeze every time Manu, then sixteen, fought for a breath. Kelepi remembers the frantic drive, his own knuckles white on the steering wheel, and the paralyzing feeling of uselessness in the emergency room. He had stood by the door, a spectator to his own son's fight for life, while a team of strangers in scrubs worked with an urgency that felt like an accusation. He was the father; he was supposed to protect his son, and in that critical moment, all he could do was watch. He had come to believe he should have seen it coming, that he had missed some sign, that his failure to act sooner was the reason Manu had come so close to death.

This sense of failure now permeates every corner of his life. At work, where he was once known for his decisive leadership, he is plagued by a profound self-doubt. He second-guesses every decision, rereading emails a dozen times before sending, certain he can no longer trust himself to do the right thing. Delays, once a simple logistical challenge, have become sources of acute dread. When a contractor’s email takes an hour longer than expected to arrive, Kelepi doesn't feel impatience; he feels a cold, sickening certainty that something catastrophic has occurred, and that it is, once again, his fault for not foreseeing it. He has built his professional life around control and planning, but he now feels he has no control at all. To cope, he fills every waking moment. His work calendar is a fortress of back-to-back meetings, and his evenings are spent meticulously planning home improvement projects he never starts. The goal is constant mental motion, a relentless forward pace to outrun the silence where the images and sounds of that night reside.

The world outside his carefully managed office has become a landscape of potential threats. A chance encounter with one of Manu's respiratory therapists in the grocery store last year sent a jolt of ice through his veins, leaving him breathless and trembling in the frozen food aisle. Since then, he avoids that part of town. He has re-routed his commute to add fifteen minutes to his drive, all to avoid the sight of the hospital. The most terrifying trigger, however, comes from within. Any hint of his own breathlessness—walking up a flight of stairs too quickly, a mild seasonal allergy—plunges him back into the horror of that night. His own chest tightens, his heart pounds, and for a moment, he is no longer a man in his sixties but a helpless father listening to his son suffocate.

For two years, Kelepi has tried to push it all down, to keep his mind so occupied that the memories have no room to breathe. He has steadfastly refused to go for his own annual physical, the thought of a stethoscope on his chest or the sterile smell of an examination room being unbearable. It was Manu himself who finally forced the issue. Two weeks ago, his son sat him down. "Dad, you look exhausted," he'd said, his voice gentle. "And you haven't seen Dr. Evans since before... everything. I'm worried about you." Seeing that look of concern on his son’s face—the very person he felt he had failed so profoundly—was the one thing that could cut through his avoidance. Kelepi is here now, not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he cannot bear the thought of failing his son again. What frightens him most is the deeply held conviction that the event happened because of who he is, and what he hopes for, in a whisper he can barely acknowledge, is to one day trust himself to keep his family safe again.
